title: Zero and first conditional
tagline: Things that are always true, and real plans for the future.
why: Zero and first conditional are everywhere at A2: school rules, the weather, real plans for the weekend. Reading Part 5 tests the grammar directly, and in Speaking you often need to say what happens next. Learn one simple rule — present after if, will only in the result — and these sentences become automatic.

hook.text: Lunchtime. Dark clouds outside. Sofia says: "If it rains, we can't play outside." Liam checks his phone. "When it rains here, it always stops fast. But if it doesn't stop, we'll go to the gym instead."
hook.ask: These if sentences mean two different things — one is always true, and one is a real plan for today. Can you find both?

use.point: Zero conditional: facts and rules that are always true

examples.text: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
examples.note: a fact about colours — always true

examples.text: When the sun goes down, it gets dark.
examples.note: when = if, for things that always happen

examples.text: If Miss Vega sees your phone in class, she takes it.

use.point: First conditional: real possibilities in the future

examples.text: If it doesn't rain, we'll play football after school.
examples.note: a real plan for later today

examples.text: She'll pass the test if she studies tonight.
If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.

use.point: Unless, and other ways to finish the result

examples.text: Unless you bring your homework, Miss Vega won't be happy.
If you're tired, go to bed early.
examples.note: imperative instead of will — an instruction

examples.text: If you finish your work, you can go outside.
examples.note: can instead of will — a permission
if-clause first → comma before the result

watch_out.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay inside.
watch_out.why: No will in the if-clause — only the present simple.

watch_out.wrong: If you mixed blue and yellow, you get green.
watch_out.right: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
watch_out.why: Zero conditional needs the present simple in both parts, not the past.

watch_out.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late.
watch_out.why: Unless already means 'if not' — don't add another negative.

watch_out.wrong: If it rains we'll stay inside.
watch_out.right: If it rains, we'll stay inside.
watch_out.why: Put a comma when the if-clause comes first.

watch_out.wrong: If she will study, she'll pass.
watch_out.why: Present simple after if — will only lives in the result.

watch_out.wrong: When it rains, it will get cold.
watch_out.why: For something that is always true, use present simple in both parts, not will.

l1.es: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.
l1.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay at home.
l1.right: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
l1.why: Spanish uses the future in both parts; English never puts will after if.

l1.wrong: When it rains, it will make cold.
l1.why: English uses get + adjective for a change, not make.

l1.es: A menos que estudies, no aprobarás.
l1.wrong: Unless you don't study, you won't pass.
l1.why: Unless already has a negative meaning — a second not is a mistake.

l1.es: Cuando termino la tarea, veo la tele.
l1.wrong: If I finish my homework, I watch TV.
l1.right: When I finish my homework, I watch TV.
l1.why: For something you always do, use when, not if — if means it might not happen.

l1.es: Iré a la fiesta si me invitan.
l1.wrong: I go to the party if they invite me.
l1.right: I'll go to the party if they invite me.
l1.why: The result needs will for a real future plan, not the present simple.

remember.trick: IF + present now, WILL in the end!
remember.tip: After if, always use the present — even when you mean the future. Save will for the result.

dialogue.title: Ice, science and Saturday's match
dialogue.context: In science class, Miss Vega's group experiments with ice while planning Saturday's football match.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: OK, everyone — if you heat ice, what happens?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It melts! If you heat it, it always melts.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Easy! Now can we talk about Saturday? If it doesn't rain, we'll play football.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: And if it rains? We can't play on a wet field.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Unless it stops before ten, we'll move the match to Sunday.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good thinking! Remember: if plus present, will in the result.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: So... if the ice melts fast, does that mean it's warm in here?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Ha! If you ask too many questions, we'll be here all day!

items.sentence: If you heat ice, it ___.
items.why: zero conditional: present simple in the result

items.sentence: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay inside.
___ you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.
If she studies hard, she ___ the exam.
items.why: first conditional: will + base verb in the result

items.sentence: When the school bell ___, everyone goes home.
items.why: zero conditional with when: present simple

items.sentence: If it's sunny tomorrow, we ___ a picnic.
items.why: a real plan for the future

items.sentence: If you mix red and white, you ___ pink.
items.why: zero conditional with you: base form, no -s

items.sentence: Call me if you ___ late.

can_do: I can talk about things that are always true with if/when + present simple.
I can talk about real future plans with if + present simple, will/won't.
I can use unless to mean 'if not' in a sentence.
summary: Zero conditional (if/when + present simple, present simple) is for things that are always true.
First conditional (if + present simple, will/won't) is for real possibilities in the future.
Never put will after if — the if-clause always uses the present simple.
Unless means 'if not' — don't add another negative after it.
Put a comma when the if-clause comes first; no comma is needed when it comes second.
